newsitem.title: USA: Low wheat supply expected in USDA stocks report.
newsitem.headline: Low wheat supply expected in USDA stocks report.

text.p: Wheat supplies in the U.S. may be the lowest in two decades because high-priced corn this summer prompted active feeding to livestock, analysts said.
"I believe it's the lowest since 1974," said Sid Love, of Kropf-Love Consulting, of his wheat stocks estimate of 1.734 billion bushels as of September 1.

USDA will release its grain and soybean stocks report at 0730CDT/1230GMT Monday. The average of analysts' estimates suggest the USDA report may show September 1 wheat stocks at 1.767 billion bushel, corn stocks at 413 million and soybeans at 163 million.
A year ago there was 1.881 billion bushels of wheat, 1.558 billion of corn and 335 million of soybeans in U.S. grain bins as of September 1.

The tight U.S. wheat situation has most analysts confident the U.S. Agriculture Department will resist using Export Enhancement Program wheat subsisidies to combate recently instituted to subsidies by the European Union.
"I don't think we have the bullets to fight a trade war this year," said Dave Armstrong, analyst with Chicago Corp. "We don't have the (EEEP) budget and we don't have the wheat."

The average corn estimate of 413 million bushels is slightly higher than USDA's ending stocks estimate of 409 million released September 11. Some analysts said high corn prices this summer caused a greater reduction in feed use than what USDA estimated in its September 11 report.
"If there is a surprise (in corn stocks) it will be a bearish surprise," said Charlie Sernatinger, analyst with Man International, who estimated September 1 corn stocks at 435 million bushels.
The average soybean estimate of 163 million bushels was near USDA's September 11 estimate of 170 million, and analysts doubt there would be a surprise in that catagory of USDA's report Monday.
